Clinical Vignette: Rajesh

Rajesh sits in the waiting room of his office building most mornings now, arriving an hour before his first patient appointment. He tells himself it's to review his notes, but really he's watching the lobby entrance, counting the security cameras, noting which exits lead where. At thirty-seven, he's spent the last fifteen years building a respected private practice specializing in anxiety disorders—a career choice that once felt like an extension of his genuine desire to help others. Today, the irony isn't lost on him.

Three months ago, Rajesh was at a shopping mall with his wife Priya on a Saturday afternoon. They'd planned it as a rare moment away from work—he'd been meaning to buy new glasses, and she wanted to visit a bookstore. They were walking past the fountain near the food court when the first explosion came. The sound was so loud it seemed to come from inside his own body. Rajesh remembers the specific detail of a child's balloon drifting past his face as people began screaming. He remembers pushing Priya down, his body covering hers, the smell of smoke and burning plastic. The second explosion came minutes later, though it felt simultaneous—time had fractured into something unreliable.

The actual physical injuries were relatively minor: Rajesh had a laceration on his shoulder from flying glass, some bruising on his ribs from being crushed against the ground. Priya was unharmed. But the internal landscape shifted in ways that no X-ray could capture.

For the first week, Rajesh told everyone he was fine. He didn't sleep much, but he attributed that to adrenaline. By week two, he'd returned to work—he felt he owed it to his patients, many of whom were themselves managing trauma. During sessions, he found himself hypervigilant in new ways, hyper-aware of the office windows, the locked door, whether he could reach it quickly. He'd always been a good listener; now he was listening for sounds. A car backfiring outside sent him rigid in his chair last Tuesday. A patient mentioned a loud noise from construction, and Rajesh's heart had begun racing before he could stop it.

Sleep has become something that happens in fragments. When he does sleep, he's back in the mall—sometimes the explosion happens differently, sometimes Priya is hurt, sometimes he can't find her at all. He wakes gasping, and Priya reaches for him, but her touch sometimes makes him flinch without meaning to. The shame of that flinch lingers longer than the nightmare itself.

He's started canceling patient appointments, something he never did before. Not officially—he reschedules them—but the pattern is clear to him, even if he hasn't admitted it to anyone else. He tells himself he's protecting his patients from his compromised attention, but the truth is more complicated: sitting with other people's pain feels impossible when his own nervous system is screaming that danger is imminent.

The news triggers him predictably now. He's stopped checking his phone for updates about the investigation. He avoids the shopping district entirely, taking longer routes to places he needs to go. Priya suggested therapy—gently, carefully, knowing the complicated position he's in as a clinician—and he's been considering it. The thought of sitting across from a colleague, admitting that his mind has turned against him, that he can't seem to regulate his own fear response despite understanding exactly how fear works neurologically, creates a different kind of paralysis.

He sits in his office lobby each morning, watching people move through the world with an ease he no longer remembers possessing.
